title: Coriolanus
author: William Shakespeare
openingText: [A company of mutinous Citizens enters, carrying staves, clubs, and other weapons.]
about:
Caius Martius is a Roman patrician who has spent his life fighting for Rome and despises its common people. After he helps take the Volscian city of Corioles, his commander Cominius gives him the name Coriolanus. Back in Rome, the Senate supports him for consul. Custom requires him to put on a humble gown, show his wounds and ask the citizens for their votes. He can scarcely bring himself to ask. Two tribunes persuade the citizens to withdraw their consent. Coriolanus insults them in public and is banished from Rome.

He goes to his old enemy, the Volscian general Aufidius, and offers him a choice: kill him or give him a command. Together they march on Rome. His former general Cominius and his old friend Menenius try in turn to win him over. Finally his mother Volumnia comes to the camp with his wife Virgilia, his young son and their friend Valeria. Volumnia kneels before him and persuades him to make peace. When he returns to the Volscians, Aufidius accuses him of betrayal, and the conspirators kill him.

Written around 1608, Coriolanus is one of Shakespeare’s late tragedies. He drew on Plutarch’s account of the Roman soldier’s life. A vote in the marketplace matters as much to the plot as a battle outside the city. The hero’s courage and his contempt for the people he defends have divided audiences and inspired sharply different political readings.

angleCards.title: A hero who hates the public.
angleCards.text: Coriolanus is the Shakespeare hero who most despises the people he is supposed to serve. The play does not soften him. Watch what Shakespeare does with a tragic figure built for the audience to flinch from.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Coriolanus as Shakespeare's hardest case — a tragic hero who openly despises the common people — and see how the play handles a figure built for the audience to dislike.

angleCards.title: Mother and son.
angleCards.text: Volumnia, Coriolanus's mother, made him what he is. She is the only person in the play with any real power over him, and in the central scene she uses it. Some critics think she is the play's real protagonist.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the relationship between Coriolanus and his mother Volumnia, and decide what the play is finally saying about who shaped him and who, in the end, decides his fate.

angleCards.title: Politics as procedure.
angleCards.text: Half the play is set in the streets and forum of Rome, with tribunes, citizens, ceremonies of showing wounds, and the formal vote of consent. It is Shakespeare's most procedurally political play.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Coriolanus as Shakespeare's most procedural political play — the tribunes, the wound-showing, the popular voice — and see what it says about the mechanics of consent.

angleCards.title: Aufidius.
angleCards.text: Aufidius, the Volscian general, has fought Coriolanus a dozen times and lost. He receives him, makes use of him, and finally has him killed. He is one of Shakespeare's most interesting secondary villains.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Aufidius — Coriolanus's rival, host, and finally the instigator of his murder — as the play's mirror to its hero, and see what Shakespeare does with the two of them.

cast.name: Caius Martius Coriolanus
cast.description: A patrician soldier who has spent his life fighting for Rome and despises the Roman commons for not appreciating it. He cannot ask for anything. He cannot lie about himself. He is one of Shakespeare's most uncompromising creations and one of his hardest to act.

cast.name: Volumnia
cast.description: The Roman matron who raised Coriolanus to be exactly what he is — a warrior, contemptuous of common men, incapable of compromise. She is also the only person who can make him change his mind, and in the play's climactic scene she does.

cast.name: Menenius Agrippa
cast.description: An older senator and Coriolanus's closest political friend, the patrician who tries to soothe the people with the parable of the belly. Witty, conservative, devoted. He tries to talk Coriolanus through the political crisis and is humiliated for his trouble.

cast.name: Sicinius and Brutus
cast.description: Two newly appointed tribunes of the plebs, the play's populist opponents. They work the crowd, manoeuvre Coriolanus into losing his temper in public, and engineer his banishment. Shakespeare gives them more political competence than he gives most of the patricians.

cast.name: Tullus Aufidius
cast.description: The Volscian commander who has been fighting Coriolanus for years and losing. When Coriolanus arrives in his house in exile, Aufidius embraces him as an equal, then gradually decides he cannot survive sharing the stage with him.

cast.name: Virgilia
cast.description: Coriolanus’s quiet wife speaks little, and different generations have read her silences differently. In Act 5 she joins Volumnia’s appeal for Rome. When Volumnia says her son must march over the womb that bore him, Virgilia reminds him who bore his own child.

acclaim.quote: Coriolanus may be not as “interesting” as Hamlet, but it is, with Antony and Cleopatra, Shakespeare’s most assured artistic success.
acclaim.context: Hamlet and His Problems, in The Sacred Wood, 1920

acclaim.quote: CORIOLANUS is a storehouse of political common-places.

whyItMatters.title: A Tragic Hero Designed to Repel
whyItMatters.body: Coriolanus is the Shakespeare tragedy that most refuses to flatter its audience. Where Hamlet is sympathetic by being articulate and Lear is sympathetic by being ruined, Coriolanus stays sympathetic to almost no one. He calls the commoners 'curs,' 'fragments,' 'scabs,' 'cowards' — and means it, all five acts. He grudgingly asks the people for their votes but refuses to show them his wounds. He goes over to the enemy because he cannot endure home. He turns back from the attack on Rome and dies because his mother kneels and he cannot live with the choice either way. Shakespeare is doing something none of the other tragedies do: he is asking what to make of a man who would rather be honest than live, and who is honest about beliefs we want him not to have. It is the play that scholars and directors fight over most, because the same Coriolanus has been claimed across the political spectrum: Brecht read him one way, the Fascist regimes another, modern directors a third. The play resists each reading because the central figure is unbending. He is what he is. The tragedy is that what he is cannot live in Rome.

whyItMatters.title: The Most Political Play
whyItMatters.body: For much of Acts 2 and 3, a Roman election drives the action. The Senate votes; the tribunes confer; the citizens debate in the streets; Coriolanus is required by custom to stand in the marketplace wearing the gown of humility and show the people his wounds. The play stages a constitutional question — what does Rome owe its commons, what does the army owe Rome, what is the relationship between popular consent and patrician honour — and refuses to settle it. Shakespeare lets us see how the votes are won and lost, person by person. There are no battles inside Rome after Act 1. There are votes, motions, manipulations, mob scenes, and a long argument about whether a great soldier owes the city anything beyond his sword. The play has been read as a critique of populism, of patrician arrogance, of the very institution of Roman government, and of all three at once. It is the play in Shakespeare where political philosophy is the action.

whyItMatters.title: The Scene with His Mother
whyItMatters.body: In Act 5, Scene 3, Coriolanus is camped outside Rome. His former general Cominius and his friend Menenius have each tried to persuade him to spare the city. Now he sees his wife approaching, then his mother holding his young son’s hand. Volumnia asks him, in front of his Volscian allies, to make peace. His family kneels. He still holds out. Only when his mother prepares to leave does the stage direction give him a gesture without words: “Holds her by the hand, silent.” A family argument has unfolded in front of Aufidius, whose trust Coriolanus risks losing with every word. When Coriolanus finally speaks, he tells his mother that her victory may cost him his life. He makes peace anyway. Soon after his return to the Volscians, the conspirators kill him.
